name: Acehnese
summary: Speakers of a Chamic language related to Cham of Vietnam; heirs of Pasai and the Aceh sultanate, the 'Veranda of Mecca'.

impacts.text: Ancestors of Acehnese speakers probably arrived from the Champa coast; date uncertain.
Samudra-Pasai is the first Muslim sultanate in the archipelago.
Aceh Darussalam grows on pepper and Islamic scholarship, rivals Portuguese Melaka.
The Aceh War: decades of Dutch conquest and guerrilla resistance.
GAM rebellion; tsunami (2004); Helsinki peace and special autonomy (2005).

name: Minangkabau
summary: A matrilineal Muslim society of the West Sumatran highlands, famous for merantau (migration) and for combining adat with Islam.

impacts.text: Coffee and trade boom; the Padri reform movement and the Dutch Padri War.
Forced coffee cultivation and colonial 'adat' administration; Ombilin coal mines worked by convicts.
Minangkabau migrants and intellectuals (Hatta, Sjahrir, Tan Malaka) prominent in nationalism.

name: Javanese
summary: The largest ethnic group in Southeast Asia, heirs of Mataram, Majapahit and Islamic Mataram, and of a long agrarian court culture.

impacts.text: Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms: Mataram (Borobudur, Prambanan), Kediri, Singhasari, Majapahit.
North-coast Muslim ports; inland Islamic Mataram.
Java War; the Cultivation System's forced export crops.
Indentured to Deli and Suriname as coolies.
Mobilised as romusha by the Japanese.
Moved as transmigrants to the outer islands — often onto indigenous land.

name: Sundanese
summary: The people of West Java, heirs of Tarumanagara, Sunda-Pajajaran and Banten.

impacts.text: Tarumanagara inscriptions of King Purnavarman.
Banten sultanate's pepper trade.
Priangan coffee under forced cultivation.

name: Balinese
summary: A Hindu society whose court culture inherited Majapahit's; later made into the archetype of 'cultural tourism'.

impacts.text: After Majapahit's fall, Hindu-Javanese court culture continues in Gelgel and Klungkung.
Balinese courts export war captives as slaves to Batavia and beyond.
Puputan: the royal houses of Badung and Klungkung die facing Dutch troops.
Tourism produces a 'touristic culture'.

name: Makassarese
summary: Seafaring people of Gowa–Tallo, whose port of Makassar was the free-trading rival of the VOC.

impacts.text: Rulers of Gowa–Tallo accept Islam.
Makassar flourishes as an open spice port.
Defeat by the VOC and Bone; diaspora.
Trepang voyages to Aboriginal Australia (Marege').

name: Bugis
region: South Sulawesi; diaspora across the archipelago
summary: Rice farmers, traders and sailors of South Sulawesi with a written literature (La Galigo) and a far-flung 18th-century diaspora.

impacts.text: Islamised by Gowa in war.
Arung Palakka of Bone allies with the VOC against Gowa.
Bugis dynasties rise in Riau, Selangor and Johor.

name: Sumbanese (Kambera, East Sumba)
summary: East Sumbanese, speakers of Kambera, in a ranked society of nobles, commoners and hereditary servants, with the Marapu ancestral religion and horse and textile trade.

impacts.text: Sumba raided and traded for slaves and horses via Ende, Bima and Makassar.
Dutch military 'pacification'; colonial rajas and districts.
Protestant missions, state land categories and, recently, plantation and tourism frontiers.

name: Dani (Baliem Valley)
summary: Highland Papuan farmers of the Baliem Valley, heirs of one of the world's independent agricultural traditions, first contacted by outsiders in 1938.

impacts.text: New Guinea highlanders domesticate taro and bananas (Kuk).
Integration into Indonesia via the New York Agreement and Act of Free Choice.
Missions, migration from other islands and militarisation; Papuan nationalism.

name: Semai (Senoi Orang Asli)
summary: The largest Orang Asli group, Senoi swidden farmers speaking an Aslian (Austroasiatic) language.

impacts.text: Mix of Hòabìnhian foragers and incoming Austroasiatic farmers.
Orang Asli communities raided for slaves by Malay and other slavers.
Forced resettlement during the Malayan Emergency.
Governed under the Aboriginal Peoples Act; land lost to plantations and dams.

name: Orang Rimba (Kubu)
region: Bukit Duabelas and Bukit Tigapuluh forests, Jambi
summary: Forest-dwelling hunter-gardeners of Jambi who speak a Malayic language and keep a strict boundary between forest life and settled outsiders; 'Kubu' is a pejorative exonym.

impacts.text: Forest-product collectors in the hinterland of Melayu/Muara Jambi.
Logging, transmigration settlements and oil palm encircle their forests.
Bukit Duabelas declared a national park.

name: Malay
region: Straits of Malacca, coasts of Sumatra and Borneo
summary: A language and court culture spread through trade and Islam — 'Malayu' identity absorbed many origins.

impacts.text: Old Malay inscriptions of Srivijaya.
Melaka sets the model of Malay Muslim kingship.
The Anglo-Dutch treaty splits the Malay world.
Defined in Malaysia's constitution as Muslim, Malay-speaking, following Malay custom.

name: Jahai (Semang Orang Asli)
summary: Semang foragers who carry the deepest local (Hòabìnhian) ancestry in mainland Southeast Asia.

impacts.text: Descend largely from early forager populations.
Pulled into the Emergency by both sides.

name: Batek (Semang Orang Asli)
region: Pahang and Kelantan, around Taman Negara
summary: Semang foragers and traders of forest products.

impacts.text: Logging and the national park reshape their territory.

name: Temiar (Senoi Orang Asli)
summary: Senoi swiddeners famous in anthropology for dream and trance practices.

impacts.text: Courted by communists and the British during the Emergency.

name: Temuan (Proto-Malay Orang Asli)
summary: Malayic-speaking Orang Asli, classified as 'Proto-Malay'.

impacts.text: Land taken for highways and the airport; landmark customary land case won in 2002.

name: Jakun (Proto-Malay Orang Asli)
summary: Malayic-speaking Orang Asli of the southern Peninsula.

name: Ayta Magbukon
summary: A Philippine Negrito people descended from the earliest settlers of the islands.

impacts.text: Ancestors among the first arrivals in the Philippines; highest known Denisovan ancestry.

name: Amis (Pangcah)
summary: Taiwan's largest indigenous people, speakers of a Formosan language from the Austronesian homeland.

impacts.text: Taiwan is the source of the Austronesian expansion.
Dutch rule and Han Chinese settlement begin to marginalise Taiwan's indigenous peoples.

name: Tagalog
summary: The people of Manila's hinterland, converted to Catholicism under Spain and central to the 1896 revolution.

impacts.text: Spanish rule centred on Manila.
Philippine Revolution.

name: Tausug
summary: Muslim people of the Sulu sultanate, which resisted Spain for three centuries.

impacts.text: Sulu sultanate trades sea and forest products for China, relying on slave raids.

name: Iban
summary: Malayic-speaking Dayak swidden farmers whose migrations and headhunting raids shaped Borneo; levies for the Brooke Raj.

impacts.text: Recruited and also fought by the Brooke Rajahs.
Logging and plantations transform longhouse lands.

name: Ngaju Dayak
summary: Barito-speaking Dayak of Central Kalimantan, with the Kaharingan religion.

impacts.text: State forest, logging, then oil palm and the failed Mega Rice Project.

name: Kenyah
region: Upper Baram and Apo Kayan, central Borneo
summary: Longhouse-dwelling stratified societies of central Borneo.

impacts.text: Resettlement and logging in the interior.

name: Ma'anyan
summary: Barito Dayak whose language is the closest relative of Malagasy.

impacts.text: Barito speakers sail to Madagascar.

name: Malagasy
summary: The westernmost Austronesians, descended from Island Southeast Asian and African ancestors.

impacts.text: Founded partly by a small group of Indonesian women.

name: Cham
summary: Austronesian people of the former kingdom of Champa, now Muslim and Hindu (Balamon) communities.

impacts.text: Kingdom of Champa on the coast of today's Vietnam.
Vijaya falls to Đại Việt.

name: Kodi (West Sumba)
summary: West Sumbanese domain studied by Janet Hoskins, with calendrical rites (the Nale festival) and exchange.

impacts.text: Exposure to slave raiding.
Colonial pacification and a new calendar of history.

name: Laboya / Lamboya (West Sumba)
summary: A West Sumbanese domain and language (Laboya), with Marapu ancestral houses and the Nale festival.

impacts.text: Colonial and Indonesian state administration redraws domains into districts.

name: Biak
family: Austronesian › Malayo-Polynesian › South Halmahera–West New Guinea
summary: Austronesian seafarers of northern Papua, long linked to Tidore and its raiding networks.

impacts.text: Agents and victims in the Tidore tribute and slave system.
Biak massacre after a Morning Star flag-raising.

name: Ternateans
summary: Speakers of a non-Austronesian (West Papuan) language; rulers of the clove sultanate of Ternate.

impacts.text: Muslim clove sultanate; Portuguese fort (1522) and expulsion (1575).

name: Bandanese (Banda Eli, Kei)
region: Banda Eli & Banda Elat, Kei Islands
summary: Descendants of Bandanese who fled the VOC conquest of 1621, still speaking a Banda language in Kei.

impacts.text: VOC conquest of Banda; mass killing, enslavement and flight.
Exile community keeps memory of the lost islands.

name: Tetum
summary: Timor's lingua franca, official language of Timor-Leste.

impacts.text: Timorese lords, Topasses and Portuguese contest sandalwood.
Indonesian occupation.

name: Atoni (Uab Meto)
summary: Dawan/Atoni Pah Meto of West Timor.

impacts.text: Divided between VOC Kupang and Portuguese-Topass spheres.

name: Toba Batak
summary: Highland people of North Sumatra, largely Protestant since 19th-century German missions.

impacts.text: Plantation belt expands onto lands of Batak and Malay cultivators.

name: Amungme
summary: Highland people whose sacred mountain became the Freeport mine.

impacts.text: Freeport mine; displacement, pollution and militarisation.

name: Kamoro
summary: Sago-forest and river people of the Mimika coast, downstream of Freeport's tailings.

impacts.text: Tailings and the mining town of Timika transform their rivers and estuaries.

name: Marind
summary: Lowland people of south Papua, at the centre of transmigration and the MIFEE agribusiness project.

impacts.text: Dutch post at Merauke; epidemics in the early 20th century.
MIFEE and food-estate concessions on Marind land.

name: Madurese
region: Madura and East Java; migrants in Kalimantan
summary: People of Madura, many of whom migrated to East Java and Kalimantan, including as transmigrants.

impacts.text: Violent conflicts with Dayak (and Malay) communities in West Kalimantan (1996–97, 1999) and Central Kalimantan (2001).

name: Yolŋu
summary: Aboriginal clans of Arnhem Land with centuries of contact with Makassan trepangers.

impacts.text: Descendants of the first peoples of Sahul.
Trade and exchange with Makassan trepangers.
Northern Territory authorities (then under South Australia) end Makassan voyages.

name: Toraja (Sa'dan)
summary: Highland rice farmers famous for tongkonan houses and funeral feasts, largely Protestant since Dutch missions.

impacts.text: Highlanders raided for slaves by lowland Bugis.
